opening.headline: The reason why previous context is lost or costs skyrocket as a conversation becomes longer is explained by the structure of the message and where the conversation state is placed.
body: If you say to the chatbot, “I have two dogs,” and then ask, “How many paws are there in the house?” and the model asks back, it looks like the model has forgotten the previous conversation. However, if you modify it to send all of the previous conversations each time, the cost will skyrocket as tokens will be increased for each request.

In this lesson, we'll first see what requests and responses from the Messages API look like, and compare how the app stores conversation state versus how the API side stores it. We distinguish the pros and cons of each method and follow the process of reading and fixing requests that have lost context.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the request/response structure and conversation state management of the message API
You can distinguish between pros and cons depending on where the status is stored.

screens.title: As the conversation became longer, context disappeared and costs soared.
screens.lead: Read the scene below to see when each of the two problems appears. Notice that fixing one problem creates another problem.

visual.alt: As the number of conversation turns increases, the request size bar becomes longer.
labels: I’m asking again because I don’t know the previous conversation.
Costs skyrocket as the number of tokens sent per request increases significantly.

paragraphs: In the first turn, the user said, “I have two dogs,” and the model responded normally. In the second turn, when asked “How many feet does a house have?”, the model asked back as if she was unaware of the previous conversation. To the developer, it looks like the model has forgotten what it just said.

The developers fixed the app so that all previous conversations were sent together each time, and the context returned. However, after about 20 turns of conversation, the number of tokens sent for each request increased significantly, causing a sharp increase in costs. This is because resending all previous conversations results in longer requests as turns accumulate.

The root of both problems is the same. Who keeps the previous conversation content, or conversation state, that the model will reference in the next response. The question for this lesson is how to decide where to store it.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Did the model really forget the previous conversation? By the end of the lesson, you will be able to answer this question accurately.

screens.outro: First, let's recall where the state of my app is.

screens.title: Where do I store conversation state?
screens.lead: As you select each storage location, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First, think about which side your app is closer to. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Storage location A: My app collects old messages and resends them each time
items.answer: The app directly holds the conversation records and sends them with each request. Instead of giving the app full control over the content of the recording, the requests become longer and longer. This method is called client state.

items.prompt: Storage Location B: The API side remembers the previous response and continues with the ID.
items.answer: The API connects the records by simply passing the identifier of the previous response. The request is short and simple to implement, but it is difficult for the app to edit the content directly. This method is called server state.

items.prompt: Which of the two methods costs less?
items.answer: It is often assumed that the server side is cheaper, but this is not the case. Either way, the model reads the previous input, and the input tokens read have a cost attached. Confirm this point with evidence in the following screen.

screens.outro: First, let's check the basic structure of the message.

screens.title: Message Structure: What Requests and Responses Look Like
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the request body and response appearance from the three providers. Although the names are different, the basic unit of alternating between user and assistant is the same.

visual.alt: A table showing how the request fields of the three providers correspond to each other.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: A request from the Claude Messages API has an array `messages`, where each message is `role`, `user`, or `assistant`. System instructions are sent to the top-level `system` parameter, not to the `system` role. The response `role` becomes `assistant`, with blocks `content` and `stop_reason` (e.g. `end_turn`), `usage`. `usage` contains the number of input and output tokens and is used to check costs when the conversation is long.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: The OpenAI Responses API puts a string or message array into `input`. The higher-level instructions are given as `instructions`. In the response, the generated content is stored in the `output` array, and can be conveniently read as `output_text` in the SDK. According to the documentation, `instructions` only applies to the current request, and if you continue with `previous_response_id`, `instructions` from the previous turn will not remain in the context.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini Interactions API sends `input` and sets the model's behavior to `system_instruction`. The result is read as `output_text`. Multi-turn dialogues are created by cascading interactions with `previous_interaction_id`. A turn is an interaction, and by default the API manages the conversation history.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body: All three providers use a structure of alternating user messages and model messages as the basic unit of conversation. The difference lies in who keeps the field names and state. You can find the field names in the document, but where to place the state is a design decision and will be covered separately in the screen that follows.

screens.outro: Now that we have the structure in place, let's first read the code to see how the app holds its state.

screens.title: Client Status: Send full history every time
screens.lead: Read the third request from the Claude Messages API. In the explanation on the right, you can see what each line determines and the symptoms that appear when it is missing.

notes.note: This line determines which model will read and how much output will be allowed. `max_tokens` is a limit on the length of the output; if this value is too small, the answer will be cut off but previous input will not be truncated.
It's the first turn. The Messages API is stateless, so if you send it without this line, the model will not know that there was a greeting.

This is the previous model answer. According to the documentation, it's okay for it to be a synthetic assistant message rather than an actual response from Claude. This means that the app has direct control over the recording.
This is the question. Without the first two lines, this would be a single question rather than a conversation.

Number of input tokens. In this example, the input for the first request was 12, but as the record builds, the input for this request is 30. As the number of turns increases, this value increases, which is why the cost increases.

screens.outro: The advantage is control, the disadvantage is longer requests. Now let's look at the other side, the server status.

screens.title: Server status and previous_response_id
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the request body changes. In server status, the entire record is changed to a single ID line, but there are also things to be careful about.

states.label: client status
states.body: The app holds on to all previous messages and sends them as an array to `input` with each request. The OpenAI documentation describes this as a way to directly manage conversation state, with requests at each turn being independent and stateless. The request includes the first question, first answer, and this question. Apps can freely edit records and are transparent about which data is being passed to the model. Instead, as the number of turns increases, the request becomes longer and the code becomes more complex.

states.label: server status
states.body: OpenAI creates a conversation by chaining responses by passing the ID of the previous response as `previous_response_id` to the next request. The Conversations API stores conversations as persistent objects with separate identifiers, making them usable across sessions, devices, and tasks. The Gemini Interactions API connects interactions with `previous_interaction_id` and the conversation history is managed by the API. The request is shortened to a new question and one line ID. There are two things to note: Previous input tokens on the chain are still billed as input tokens, their content is difficult for apps to edit directly, and relies on retention policies.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen both methods, let's summarize the pros and cons at a glance.

screens.title: Analysis: Pros and Cons of State Storage Locations
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to follow how the instructor compares the two methods. The selection criteria in the last row are key.

data.caption: Comparison of client archiving and server archiving
rows: The app takes full control of all your messages. You are free to edit, summarize, and delete.
Because the API side manages the history, it is difficult for apps to modify the content directly.
More turns result in longer requests and more complex app code.
Since we only send a new question and ID, the request is short and simple to implement.
Since you resend the previous turn, you are charged with input tokens.
Previous input tokens in the chain are also charged as input tokens.
Accumulated records occupy the window. As the limit approaches, the app summarizes or deletes older turns.
Likewise, your previous history takes up a lot of the window, and it's difficult for the app to reduce it, limiting how you manage it.
If control and transparency are important to you, choose this.
If simplicity of implementation is important to you, choose this.
data.notes: The only difference between the two methods is who stores it, the amount of input the model reads is the same. So context window limits and input token charging have an effect one way or another. The expectation that server archiving reduces costs is an illusion created by the seemingly short request body. It is up to the app to manage client archives by summarizing or deleting old turns to reduce request size.

screens.outro: Now that we've established a baseline, let's actually read and fix the requests that have lost context.

screens.title: Commentary: Reading and fixing out-of-context requests
screens.lead: Select the arrow to the right to see your instructor follow you from symptom to confirmation. Imagine how the request body changes with each step.

steps.title: Stage 1 symptoms
steps.body: In the third turn, the user asks, “So how many feet do you have?” and the model asks what he means. Even though I said there were two dogs earlier, the model doesn't seem to know.

steps.title: Step 2: Read the request
steps.body: Look at `messages` in the request body. There is only one line, like `[{"role": "user", "content": "So how many feet does it have?"}]`. Since the previous two turns are not in the request, the information “2 puppies” is also not in the request.

steps.title: Step 3: Identify the cause
steps.body: The model hasn't forgotten. The Claude Messages API is stateless, so it only reads the content contained in this request. Because the preceding conversation was not included in the request, the model had no way of knowing.

steps.title: Step 4 Modification
steps.body: In the client method, the app sends three messages: a user message about the dog, an assistant response, and a new user question. If it's the server method, just send a new question and `previous_response_id`. Either way, the previous context will be loaded somewhere the model can read it.

steps.title: Step 5 Confirmation
steps.body: The increase in input tokens at `usage` in the response is a sign that the context has actually been passed. And either way, previous entries will be charged. As requests become larger around turn 20, separate management is done to reduce the request size, such as summarizing old turns.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished the explanation, I'll close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Where you put your state determines cost and consistency
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Check the answer to the question posed at the beginning: Did the model really forget the previous conversation?

paragraphs: Answering the first question, the model has not forgotten the previous conversation. It's just that the previous turn was not listed in `messages` of that request. The Claude Messages API is stateless, so you always have to send the entire conversation history, and the same goes for OpenAI and Gemini if ​​you don't use server archiving.

There are two places to put conversation state: Archiving by the app lengthens the request at the cost of full control and editing of the content. Server archiving makes requests shorter, simpler to implement, but relies on archiving policies and makes editing difficult. The selection criteria are whether control and transparency are important or whether simplicity is important.

Whichever method you use, the input token and context window limits have an effect. Even if you use `previous_response_id`, previous input tokens on the chain will be charged. When conversations get long, you need to take care of summarizing or deleting old turns.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The model reads only what is included in the request. If you're missing context, check the request body first.

glossary.def: This is a request format in which a user and an assistant alternately stack messages with role and content to express a conversation.
Previous conversation history that the model should reference in its next response.
The distinction is based on whether the API side stores previous conversations or whether the app stores them and resends them each time.
This is a parameter that creates a conversation by chaining responses by passing the ID of the previous response in the OpenAI Responses API.

misconceptions.myth: The API automatically remembers previous conversations.
misconceptions.fact: The Claude Messages API is stateless, so apps must send the entire history each time. The function for the server to connect records is selected and used separately.

misconceptions.myth: If you use previous_response_id, there is no previous token cost.
misconceptions.fact: Previous input tokens in the chain are also charged as input tokens and also occupy the context window. It only reduces the amount the app sends.

misconceptions.myth: Where you store the state is just a matter of convenience.
misconceptions.fact: Storage location directly impacts control, cost management, and consistency. This is a decision that must be made during the design phase.

misconceptions.myth: The model forgot the previous conversation.
misconceptions.fact: It's not that I forgot, it's that the previous turn was not included in the messages of the request. The model only reads what is included in the request.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Where you place your state determines cost and consistency.
The message API has a structure in which user and assistant messages are stacked alternately.
Client state is easy to control, and server state is simple to implement.
Either way, input tokens and context window limits have an effect.
